0700: Here is the most common way APIs leak customer data. A user opens their invoice. The request says invoice 1042. They change it to 1043, and the server sends back someone else's invoice. No hacking tools. Just a number. It happens because the app checks that you are logged in, but never checks that this record belongs to you. The fix is boring and reliable. On every request, load the record, compare its owner to the logged-in user, and refuse if they do not match. Then write a test with two users trying to read each other's data, and run it on every release.
0900: If you build software for banks or payment firms in Europe, DORA changes your security work. The Digital Operational Resilience Act has applied since January 2025. In plain words: financial firms must prove they can withstand, respond to and recover from technology incidents, including incidents at their suppliers. For engineers, that means three practical things. Know which systems support critical services. Test recovery for real, not on paper. And treat third-party services as part of your risk, with an exit plan. Teams that already work this way find DORA is mostly evidence. The rest find it is a lot of work.
1300: Your payment provider sends a webhook that says: order paid. How do you know it really came from them? If you do not check, anyone who finds your webhook URL can send the same message and get goods for free. Three checks fix it. One. Verify the signature with the secret your provider gives you, and reject anything that fails. Two. Check the amount and currency against your own order record. Never trust the payload alone. Three. Make the handler safe to run twice, because providers will send it again. Signature, amount, idempotency. Miss one, and someone eventually gets something for free.
1500: Junior security engineers report findings. Senior ones report decisions. An executive does not need the severity score. They need three things. What could happen, in business terms: a customer's money moved without consent. How likely it is, and what it would cost. And the options, with the effort each one takes. Then make a recommendation, and let them choose. The goal is not to win every argument. It is to make sure every risk the company carries, it carries on purpose.
1700: Anything you put inside a mobile app, assume an attacker can read. App files can be downloaded and unpacked in minutes. So API keys, admin tokens and payment secrets do not belong in the app. At most, the app should hold a public identifier. Everything sensitive stays on your server, and the app asks the server to do the privileged work, using the user's own session. If a key has already shipped in an app, treat it as leaked. Rotate it, restrict it, and move that work to the server.
1900: Two weeks to launch. Five security findings. And time to fix only two. So which ones go first? My rule is simple: anything that lets one user touch another user's data or money. What is yours?
